0229_Dynamic_American_City_The_23_00_35_.sy: There could be no better film than this to show how old, character-filled neighborhoods in cities across the nation were wantonly destroyed during the "new is better" 1950s. Some good shots of 50s cars on urban streets; an especially good one contrasts 50s automobiles with a turn of the century horse-drawn bakery wagon of Boston ("Albert Duplain - French Bakers") in a wistful juxtaposition of eras. Rare footage of interurban streetcars / trolleys rolling through semi-rural areas; charming Victorian looking railroad station for "Ant Hill". Freeways. Traffic. Dams. Suburban sprawl: sign on undeveloped tract reads "Coming Soon: FOOD FAIR Supermarket"; then, another sign for W.T. Grant dime store. New construction; suburban corporate headquarters are shown amid greenery. New shopping centers, the concrete barely dry. Good CUs of Victorian architectural detail; then, of course, old buildings being demolished for 50s steel and glass structures. Wrecking balls destroying old structures. Excellent shots of 1950s parking garages. Hotels, motels.

0999_Land_of_Montezuma_The_01_05_25_01.sy: This vintage travelogue presents a vivid portrait of Mexico City and its surrounding areas, highlighting both its historical grandeur and cultural richness. The film begins with a view of Chapultepec Castle, once the home of Emperor Maximilian and now a symbol of national pride. The film continues with scenes of Mexico’s elite military academy and disciplined presidential guard, emphasizing their precision and strength. Firefighters, though sharply dressed, are praised for their athleticism and modern equipment. A visit to the National Palace introduces viewers to the historic Liberty Bell, while the National Museum showcases ancient Aztec treasures like the massive stone calendar. Educational and financial progress is noted through depictions of agricultural schools and the Bank of Mexico. The downtown area, bustling with traffic and narrow streets, is portrayed as orderly and well-managed. Modernity is reflected in infrastructure, such as parks with public radios, stadiums, and recreation fields, yet only a short drive away, viewers encounter rural scenes that seem frozen in time. Indigenous women wash clothes in rivers using ancient techniques, and families offer heartfelt hospitality to strangers, sharing food and shelter with humility. The film closes with a peaceful image of a 17th-century monastery, symbolizing the enduring spirit and tranquility of the Mexican people.

SVS-1374.sy: This animation is one in a series created to show an accurate representation of the Earth's rotation at different temporal resolutions. The animation is created from images taken by the Galileo spacecraft during a close pass of the Earth on December 11-12, 1990. The animations range from real-time, in which no rotation can be perceived, to 3600 times real-time, in which both the Earth's rotation and cloud motion can bee seen. The series also includes an animation in which the Earth's rotation has been 'halted' so that cloud motion is easier to see and an animation showing the specific amount of rotation that takes place in three minutes. Note: An animation of the Earths rotation from Galileo imagery at 600 times real-time. The timer indicates hours and minutes of elapsed time. The Earths rotation is apparent, but cloud motion is not perceptible. Animator: Horace Mitchell (NASA/GSFC). Scientist: Doug Norton (NASA/HQ). Platforms/Sensors/Data Sets: Galileo/Solid-State Imaging Camera.
